proves: a backdrop filter changes what is already on the canvas behind the node, within the node's own box and nowhere else. The property was read in exactly one place before this fixture's commit - the isolation-layer question - and applied nowhere.
checkable: 264x72, twelve 22-wide stripes alternating 220,40,40 and 40,80,220 across the whole page, with three 72x56 panels of white at 25% alpha at y=8..63, at x=8, 96 and 184. Read row 36. Panel 0 (control) shows the stripes through the panel with hard edges: 229,94,94 from x=8 to 21 and 94,124,229 from x=22 to 43. Panel 1 reads 122,122,122 over what was red and 125,125,125 over what was blue - equal channels, so the colour is gone. Panel 2's first stripe edge is a ramp rather than a step: reading the red channel from x=184 upward gives 226, 229, 228, 224, 215, 200, 179, 155, 132, 113, 102, 96, 94 at two-pixel steps, where the control steps 229 to 94 between x=20 and x=22. Row 4 is above every panel and reads the stripes unchanged, 220,40,40 and 40,80,220 alternating every 22 pixels.
checkable_outside_the_panels: row 36 passes through all three panels and cannot see the clip, so read y=4 and y=68 as well - above and below the panels, in the same columns. Both rows are the untouched stripes at every column: 220,40,40 at x=12, 100 and 188, and 40,80,220 at x=30, 118 and 206. A filter applied to the page rather than to the node's box would grey or blur those columns, and no row that crosses a panel could tell.
expected: the filtered backdrop is drawn back clipped to the panel, so the stripes outside the panels are untouched and the stripes inside them are filtered. The translucent panel is then composited over the result, which is why the greyscale cell reads 122 rather than 0.
why_the_panels_are_translucent: a backdrop filter is invisible under anything opaque - the filtered backdrop is covered by the very node that asked for it. Three separate sessions probed this property against an opaque box and each read the result as drawing nothing. The obvious control is the broken one, and this fixture exists partly to record that.
why_two_filters_and_not_one: they fail differently. A colour filter that never ran leaves the stripes coloured; a blur that never ran leaves the stripe edge hard. One cell cannot show both.
why_stripes: a blur of a linear ramp is that ramp again, so a backdrop blur can be perfect and change nothing over smooth content. A hard edge is the only backdrop a blur cannot be a fixed point of. The blur's reach is also what this cell pins: the ramp is symmetric about the stripe edge because the readback is grown by three standard deviations per blur before it is filtered, and a version that reads only the panel's own box smears the edge pixel instead.
status: measured from the committed image. Backdrop filtering landed in the commit that added this fixture. Panels 1 and 2 reading the same hard-edged stripes as panel 0 is the regression it exists to catch.
